name: Zentai suit

card.summary: A full-body skin-tight suit covering head, hands and feet that hides the wearer's own features for costume, performance and anonymity.
card.note: Face-covering suits are restricted in some places and banned by some sports leagues.

quick.overview:
A zentai is a stretch fabric suit, usually nylon-spandex, that covers the whole body. The name comes from the Japanese zenshin taitsu, full-body tights.[1]

It is used for costumes, dance and fan culture, video chroma-key work and anonymity: the suit hides the wearer's face and body detail, so appearance is replaced by a uniform shape or colour.[1][2]
quick.how: Wearers pull on a one-piece or multi-piece suit in a solid colour or pattern. Uses include sports-fan costumes, dance groups, performance art and green-screen effects.[1]
quick.risks: Face-covering means some jurisdictions restrict wearing them in public; France may fine up to 150 euros, and Major League Baseball bans the hoods. Heat build-up and limited vision are practical concerns.[1]

lead: A zentai suit is a skin-tight garment covering the entire body including head, hands and feet, typically made of nylon or spandex blends. The word is short for the Japanese zenshin taitsu (全身タイツ).[1][2]
Instead of improving a wearer's features, it conceals them. Wearers describe it as a way to become anonymous, to escape social pressure about appearance, or to perform as a character.[2]

Uniform look for costume, performance or anonymity
angle.text: A zentai works by concealment: it removes visible facial and body features, which wearers use for costumes and for relief from self-consciousness.

paras: Documented uses include sports fans (the Vancouver Canucks 'Green Men'), street-dance groups, chroma-key video work where the solid colour is digitally removed, music videos, fashion, public art and social-anxiety workshops.[1]
In Japan, some wearers describe using zentai to reduce pressure about personal appearance by obscuring features.[2]

France may fine wearers up to 150 euros for face-covering in public, and some sports leagues ban the hoods.[1] The suits are also associated by some with fetish communities, though wearers and event organisers describe broader artistic and costume use.[2]
